slides.title: Today’s sequence
table: Setup, data model, and a repeatable operation
Inspect the workflow and its limits
Then keep the assessment–UX–testing sequence together
Record a first judgment, then reconsider it
Three reviews, one priority change, one retest
slides.notes: Today we will connect the Python work you know from Maya to Unreal’s editor. Look at the whole task, not only the code. After the break, you will assess a tool before we discuss UX principles, then immediately apply those principles to a classmate’s tool.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: What you should be able to explain
bullets: Which objects a tool will affect
How you will inspect and verify its result
How another artist can use it without your help
slides.question: What would make you trust a tool with your project?
slides.notes: By the end, you should be able to explain scope, evidence, and the user’s task. A script finishing without an exception is only one part of success. Keep one tool from your own work in mind as we go.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Tools are part of game production
slides.credit: Guerrilla · Sumaili & van der Steen · GDC 2017 · PDF p.23
slides.notes: This is Guerrilla’s Decima level editor, shown in its Horizon Zero Dawn pipeline talk. The class-sized question is smaller: which repeated step prevents an artist from checking their work? Keep that task in view as we learn a new host API.
slides.question: Which repeated task would you remove from this workflow?
slides.rationale: Place a real production editor before API details to establish the purpose of tooling.

slides.title: Python across applications
bullets: Keep loops, functions, conditions, and data structures
Replace Maya commands with Unreal editor APIs
Carry over explicit inputs, scope, and useful reports
slides.question: Which part of your Maya tool is independent of Maya?
slides.notes: Your general Python knowledge carries over. The objects and operations exposed by the host application change. Keep reusable rules separate from host-specific operations where practical. Here, unreal is the module exposed by the editor; installing ordinary Python alone does not create an Unreal editor session.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Python setup in Unreal
bullets: Enable Python Editor Script Plugin
Enable Editor Scripting Utilities; restart the editor
Choose Python input mode in Output Log
slides.question: Is the input field running Python or console commands?
slides.notes: Enable these plugins for the project you are using and restart. Switch the Output Log input to Python. Unreal supplies its embedded interpreter; do not assume your terminal interpreter has the same modules. We are using Python for editor automation, not runtime gameplay.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: First execution
bullets: Output Log: choose Python
Saved file: File > Execute Python Script
slides.question: What evidence tells you the script ran in the intended project?
slides.notes: Run the small logging example first. Then execute a saved script. Project Content/Python is one of the supported search locations. A saved file gives us something we can inspect, revise, and rerun. Watch the Output Log rather than assuming silence means success.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Unreal’s object model
table: A Static Mesh in the Content Browser
May be referenced by many placements
One placed crate in the level
Has its own label and transform
References the mesh and can hold overrides
slides.question: If two Actors share a mesh, which edits could affect both?
slides.notes: A placed object and the asset it references are not the same thing. In our existing fixture, six prop Actors use five shared mesh assets. Editing an Actor transform is different from changing the shared asset. A component can also carry a material override. Always identify which layer your operation edits.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Shared asset, separate placements
slides.caption: Conceptual relationship · the mesh asset can have multiple references
slides.notes: Trace both references to the same mesh asset. The Actors can have different transforms. Changing shared geometry can affect both placements. For a material change, determine whether you are changing the shared asset or a component override before building the operation.
slides.question: Where would you make a change that affects only Actor A?
slides.rationale: Make mutation scope visible before selection and editing.

slides.title: Selection is an input
bullets: Level selection is not Content Browser selection
Check eligibility before building a change plan
slides.question: What should your tool do with an empty selection?
slides.notes: This read-only example asks the editor Actor subsystem for selected level Actors. It does not retrieve selected Content Browser assets. We can report the labels before attempting any edits. Next check whether each object supports the operation and explain any skipped items.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Disk paths and Unreal asset paths
slides.question: Which path belongs in the source-file field?
slides.notes: These are illustrative paths, not files supplied with this slide. Keep the source file, destination folder, and imported object identity distinct. An import task takes a filename and a destination path. Read its resulting object paths to learn what was actually created.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Maya and Unreal handoff
slides.question: What must remain stable when the Maya source changes?
slides.notes: Treat the file handoff as the first bridge. Remote control between applications is not necessary to explain it. Make one source revision, then check that the intended Unreal asset updates. Importer behavior and settings need to be rehearsed in the engine version used for class.
slides.caption: Course schematic · file exchange and revision loop
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Explicit import settings
slides.code:
task = unreal.AssetImportTask()
task.filename = source_file
task.destination_path = "/Game/Props"
task.automated = True
task.save = False
tools = unreal.AssetToolsHelpers.get_asset_tools()
tools.import_asset_tasks([task])
bullets: Configure options for the chosen importer
Inspect imported_object_paths and the result
slides.question: What should happen when the destination already exists?
slides.notes: This is an illustrative API excerpt: source_file must name an existing input and the appropriate importer options still need configuration. Automated import suppresses interaction; it does not prove that the result matches our intent. Saving is deliberately separate here. Reimport and replacement policies require explicit choices rather than relying on this minimal snippet.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: A controlled editor operation
bullets: Collect and inspect a bounded selection
Preview exact changes before applying them
Verify results, then demonstrate recovery
slides.code:
import week07_tools as w7
w7.select_demo()
plan = w7.preview()
w7.apply(plan)
w7.check()
slides.question: What should invalidate a preview before Apply?
slides.notes: These commands belong to the existing course fixture, not the general Unreal API. Preview produces a plan; Apply should not quietly act on different inputs. The tool’s existing records document a controlled Actor-label and placement operation. Undo history is not a backup, and import recovery may require a different approach.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Blueprints as an editor interface
table: Inputs, scope, actions, and result display
Validate, perform the operation, report results
slides.question: Should the button contain the whole tool—or call one operation?
slides.notes: This is the Blueprint connection we need today. Epic supports Python execution nodes in editor-only Blueprints such as Editor Utility Widgets. The Execute Python Script node can expose custom inputs and outputs. It does not make Python a gameplay scripting language. Its execution-success output is not a substitute for checking whether the artist’s task succeeded.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: One operation, multiple interfaces
slides.caption: Course architecture sketch · alternate UI entry points
slides.notes: The UI gathers inputs and displays results. A shared operation owns the rules. An Editor Utility Widget can call that operation through an editor-only Python execution node. A Qt interface can call the same Python function. Sharing the operation helps keep the rules consistent.
slides.question: Which logic should survive a complete UI redesign?
slides.rationale: Connect Qt, Blueprint and Python without teaching a second implementation stack.

slides.title: Starting state
slides.caption: Existing course capture · Unreal 5.7.4 · six-prop fixture
slides.question: Which values can this operation change safely?
slides.notes: This is the starting state of the course fixture. The prepared operation changes Actor labels and positions, not the shared mesh assets. Predict the result before looking at the organized capture.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Result inspection
slides.caption: Existing course capture · same fixture after the controlled operation
slides.question: What does this image prove—and what still needs checking?
slides.notes: The second capture shows the arranged props. An image alone does not verify labels, selection boundaries, or recovery. Use the tool’s report and an Undo check to establish those properties. Compare the capture with the tool’s report before drawing a conclusion.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Recovery is observable behavior
slides.caption: Existing course capture · transaction entry in Unreal
slides.notes: Here is the recorded transaction for the fixture. Test recovery using the same kinds of changes you intend to teach. A transaction is useful for editor operations that participate in Undo. It does not guarantee recovery from every file export, import, or external operation.
slides.question: Which state should return after one Undo?
slides.rationale: Anchor the recovery discussion in real editor evidence.

slides.title: Tool demonstrations
bullets: Co-teacher examples · 15 minutes
TA examples · 20 minutes
For each: task, scope, result, and recovery
slides.question: Where does the artist make a decision?
slides.notes: As you watch the demonstrations, identify the task each tool supports, the scope it changes, how the result is verified, and how the artist recovers. Hold onto examples that connect to your own project. The presenter slots include their questions and handoffs.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Break
bullets: When we return: assess a tool
Then revisit your assessment through UI/UX
Apply the same thinking in peer testing
slides.notes: Take the break now. When we return, keep your initial impressions: we will use them as evidence for the discussion rather than replacing them with a checklist immediately.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Tool assessment: predict the result
slides.question: Rule: exactly one SM_ prefix on selected assets. Leave all others unchanged.
slides.notes: This is a fictional paper case, not a captured engine bug. Assign a reader, recorder, evidence checker, and reporter. Complete the expected result before seeing the output. When the result is revealed, first write your own answer: would you trust this tool, and what would you change first?
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Tool assessment: compare the evidence
slides.question: The tool says “4 assets updated.” Did the task succeed?
slides.notes: The first two rows are correct. The already-prefixed name gets another prefix, and the unselected barrel changes. Record the behavior before guessing the code cause. Recovery, performance, and a second run remain unknown. Preserve your first priority and the reason for it.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Interface and experience
bullets: UI: the controls, labels, and layout
UX: reaching the intended result in context
A successful execution can still fail the task
slides.question: Which part of your first assessment would you defend?
slides.notes: Return to the renamer. A success count did not make the task successful. Some problems were functional errors; a clearer interface cannot repair the wrong mutation. UX also includes understanding scope, finding results, and recovering. Your initial instinct may be sound. We are adding a more precise way to explain and investigate it.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: A workflow spans several tools
slides.credit: Jeff Stewart · Vicarious Visions · GDC 2018 · PDF p.9
slides.notes: Vicarious Visions used Laboratory’s World Builder for Skylanders and Crash levels. For our importer, include the artist’s export and inspection steps when defining the task. Ask where the artist comes from and where they need to go next.
slides.question: What happens immediately before and after your tool?
slides.rationale: Extend UX beyond the tool window using a documented production example.

slides.title: User stories
bullets: As an environment artist…
I want to bring a revised prop into Unreal…
So I can inspect it without rebuilding its setup.
slides.question: What would count as success for this artist?
slides.notes: This is a classroom example of role, goal, and benefit. It starts a conversation rather than specifying a particular button. Add observable acceptance checks: the intended asset updates, the result is easy to locate, and unrelated work stays unchanged. Ask the artist about their current workflow before treating the story as a verified requirement.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Sketching before implementation
bullets: Compare two approaches to one task
Include the starting state and a failure
Paper and Figma can both test an interaction
slides.question: What can a sketch test? What requires a running tool?
slides.notes: A sketch can help test interpretation and flow before implementation. Figma connects frames so a person can try a simulated interaction. It does not verify the Unreal operation. Research on parallel prototyping found benefits in an advertisement-design study; comparing layout alternatives here is our teaching application, not a measured Unreal productivity claim.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Two layouts for the same task
slides.caption: Illustrative sketches · neither layout is a tested recommendation
slides.notes: These sketches support the same import task. One keeps everything visible; the other separates decisions into steps. Predict where a novice might hesitate and where an experienced artist might want to move faster. Test that prediction before choosing a layout.
slides.question: Which prediction could a paper test resolve?
slides.rationale: Turn sketching advice into a visible comparison students can question.

slides.title: Layout follows the task
slides.caption: Detail crops from the course PySide tool · offline sample data
slides.question: Where would you look first? What is unclear?
slides.notes: This capture shows the actual PySide implementation using offline sample data. Notice the scope, before-and-after table, and named action. These features support inspection, but they still need testing with users. The backend rules remain separate from the presentation. The screenshot is not evidence of a live Unreal edit.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Mental models and visible scope
bullets: Ask what the artist expects to change
Show the target and relevant state
Use visible choices instead of remembered syntax
slides.question: Does filtering the report also change what Apply affects?
slides.notes: People bring expectations from other tools. In the captured Prop Inspector, filtering displayed rows does not change the reviewed plan; the interface states that explicitly. Ask a tester to predict scope before they act. Their explanation gives us evidence about their mental model, not proof that the implementation is correct.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: The artist’s model of the work
slides.credit: Jeff Stewart · Vicarious Visions · GDC 2018 · PDF p.35
slides.notes: Cinematic Builder presents a VFX cue as a duration, while underlying data uses spawn and kill keyframes. For a classroom tool, ask which representation helps the artist make the next decision. Internal data structures can remain in code.
slides.question: Would an artist rather edit a duration or two unrelated events?
slides.rationale: Use a concrete production UI to explain mental models.

slides.title: State and feedback
slides.caption: Detail crops from the course PySide tool · empty offline state
slides.question: What information belongs beside the action rather than in an alert?
slides.notes: Here the empty state says what to do next and the Apply action is unavailable. A disabled control still needs an explanation. After work completes, distinguish changed, skipped, and failed items. Apple’s guidance connects the level of interruption to the consequence: routine status can stay near the work, while a significant actionable risk may warrant interruption.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: An error should support recovery
slides.caption: Actual course PySide tool · offline blocked state
slides.notes: Read the message as an artist who has not seen the code. Can you identify the problem, the affected input, and the next action? A raw exception may help the developer, but the artist also needs a way to resume the task.
slides.question: What would you change in this message?
slides.rationale: Use a real practice interface as critique material rather than a claimed ideal UI.

slides.title: Recovery and accessibility
bullets: Review consequential changes before applying them
Test the recovery path you actually offer
Keep focus, labels, and status understandable
slides.code:
# Existing PySide view implementation
self.preview.setAccessibleName(
    "Selected Actors change preview"
)
slides.question: Could a classmate recover without help?
slides.notes: Recovery can mean Undo for an editor transaction, or a separate restore and reimport procedure. Do not promise that all operations can be undone. The code excerpt names the preview for accessibility; it is one implementation detail, not a complete accessibility guarantee. Check keyboard operation, visible focus, readable text, and status cues that do not rely on color alone.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Mission Kontrol: repeatable testing
slides.credit: Etienne Palmer-Campbell · NetherRealm · GDC 2025 · PDF p.46
slides.notes: Mission Kontrol lets developers request character actions without performing their button combinations. The transfer to your tool is a repeatable starting state and an action another person can reproduce independently.
slides.question: What knowledge should a tester need before starting?
slides.rationale: Connect professional Unreal tooling directly to the upcoming peer test.

slides.title: Feedback changes the interface
slides.credit: Etienne Palmer-Campbell · NetherRealm · GDC 2025 · PDF p.47
slides.notes: QA feedback led to controls for both players and frame stepping. Look for a comparable dependency in your own workflow: does using one tool require reaching for another control elsewhere? That handoff may be worth testing.
slides.question: Which nearby action would make your workflow easier to complete?
slides.rationale: Show an actual iteration outcome instead of only recommending feedback.

slides.title: Evidence before explanation
table: The tester chose the wrong destination
The destination label may be unclear
Can a new tester choose the intended target without help?
slides.question: What questions remain before we begin testing?
slides.notes: Separate what happened from why you think it happened. A preference can be useful, but it does not replace observing the task. Keep the version stable across today’s three rounds so findings can be compared. If an emergency fix is necessary, record it. Afterwards choose a change and retest. Three classmates provide useful leads, not proof that every user will succeed.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: A test produces the next question
slides.caption: Course testing loop · a possible explanation is not yet a finding
slides.notes: An observation gives you evidence. Your explanation is still a hypothesis. Make one change that addresses it and repeat the task. If the difficulty remains, revise the explanation rather than merely adding more instructions.
slides.question: What would show that your proposed change did not help?
slides.rationale: Make the observation–revision–retest loop explicit before students write tasks.

slides.title: A task another person can attempt
bullets: A goal and a small starting input
An observable result and protected scope
A reset state and an honest review mode
slides.question: Which initial judgment would you now revise—or defend—and why?
slides.notes: Write one task that can be attempted in about two minutes. For example, arrange three selected props and leave the light unchanged. State the goal rather than a click sequence. Prefill the author details and task on the short peer sheets. A prototype or recording is still useful, but label it honestly and do not report imagined behavior as observed.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Peer testing: three perspectives
bullets: Work in groups of four: A, B, C, D
Both partners test in every round
Use the author’s machine; record any help
slides.question: What will you observe before suggesting a redesign?
slides.notes: Use the prepared starting state and the same primary task in all three rounds. Do not spend the round installing a tool on someone else’s machine. If the tool cannot launch promptly, use the prepared fallback and label the review mode. Support an unfinished tool without pretending it is complete.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: A ten-minute reciprocal round
table: Author states goal, inputs, success, and safety
slides.question: Allow an attempt before coaching; record assistance when given.
slides.notes: During the attempt, observe and allow the tester to explain their expectations. Avoid telling them where to click unless help becomes necessary; if you help, record it. The final two minutes are for finishing and resetting, not expanding to an entirely new task.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Partner rotations
bullets: One minute to switch between rounds
Keep the same task and record the version
slides.question: What repeats across reviews? What depends on the reviewer?
slides.notes: Stay within your group. The rotations give each person three different reviewers. Use the same task and start state, and keep observations tied to the actual review mode. Repeated evidence may help prioritize a problem, but a single consequential failure can also deserve attention.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Your next revision
bullets: Identify one strength worth preserving
Choose one consequential improvement
Describe the evidence your retest should produce
slides.question: How did your first intuition change after observing someone else?
slides.notes: Compare the reviews before selecting a fix. Choose a change that addresses an observed difficulty, explain the reason, and describe a retest. You can also defend an initial decision if the evidence supports it. Record what remains uncertain rather than forcing a confident conclusion.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: The current project is part of the input
slides.caption: Existing course Unreal capture · project, level and Outliner context
slides.notes: Before running an edit, identify the project and level. Check what is selected in the Outliner and what the tool reports. A familiar asset name can exist in more than one project. Your tool should make its working context inspectable.
slides.question: What context would you include in a useful run report?
slides.rationale: Provide a concrete editor-context check without extending the core API introduction.

slides.title: Reimport needs a prediction
slides.notes: Before reimporting, predict one observable change and one thing that should remain stable. Then inspect both. The importer and its settings control the result, so repeat this check in the teaching project rather than assuming every asset behaves identically.
slides.question: How would you detect an unintended duplicate?
slides.rationale: Separate an import call from the evidence needed to validate the bridge.

slides.title: A preview is a temporary agreement
slides.caption: Course state model · changed inputs require a new preview
slides.notes: A preview describes a particular set of inputs. If the artist changes selection or another relevant value, the old preview may no longer describe the next edit. Invalidate it or rebuild it. After Apply, compare the actual result with the prediction.
slides.question: What else could make a preview stale?
slides.rationale: Explain why a preview button alone does not guarantee correct scope.

slides.title: Change and reset
slides.caption: Animated comparison of existing captures · not continuous execution footage
slides.notes: Watch the prepared comparison, then describe the changed values. Use the report and recovery demonstration to verify what the animation cannot show. The animation compares existing captured states; it does not show elapsed execution time.
slides.question: What can this animation show? What remains unverified?
slides.rationale: Offer an offline motion reference with honest limits.

slides.title: A click connects to an operation
slides.caption: Existing course Qt schematic · signal, callback and visible result
slides.notes: Qt emits a signal when the button is activated. A connected callback runs the operation and updates the result. This is where a UI decision becomes code: the callback can validate input, prevent duplicate work, and report the outcome.
slides.question: Where would you stop an invalid operation?
slides.rationale: Supply the requested light technical implementation tie-in.

slides.title: Warning and blocked states
slides.caption: Actual course PySide tool · offline warning state
slides.notes: A warning asks the artist to make a decision. A blocked state means a required condition is missing. Choose the behavior based on the operation’s consequence. Avoid treating every status update as an interruption.
slides.question: Can the artist proceed? What evidence supports that choice?
slides.rationale: Distinguish UI states that often collapse into generic alerts.

slides.title: Keyboard and focus
bullets: A logical Tab order follows the task
Visible focus shows the active control
Shortcuts remain discoverable
slides.notes: Try completing the task without a mouse. Track where focus moves and whether you can tell which control is active. These Qt calls illustrate focus and tab order, but the surrounding widget setup is omitted. Test the behavior in the actual application.
slides.question: Where does keyboard focus go after an error?
slides.rationale: Expand accessibility into a concrete implementation and test.

slides.title: Testing continues after release
slides.credit: Etienne Palmer-Campbell · NetherRealm · GDC 2025 · PDF p.55
slides.notes: The talk describes focused QA, a studio introduction, and continued maintenance. Our peer lab is one small iteration. After the lab, make a targeted change and run the task again with someone who did not watch you build it.
slides.question: How will users report a problem after your first release?
slides.rationale: Place classroom testing within a longer tool lifecycle.

slides.title: A useful observation record
table: Whether the label or the path caused hesitation
Whether the task wording supplied enough context
The code cause and the affected scope
slides.notes: Record the behavior and the help you gave. Avoid writing only that the tool was confusing or intuitive. A precise observation gives the author something they can investigate and gives you a basis for choosing the next test.
slides.question: Which statement could another observer verify?
slides.rationale: Give students an example of usable evidence before peer review.

slides.title: Material automation: a later connection
slides.caption: Actual practice-mode interface · sample data, no Unreal connection
slides.question: What should remain editable by the artist?
slides.notes: This local practice panel illustrates how a prepared parent material, texture inputs, a new instance, and a component assignment can be reviewed before applying. It is not a capture of a live Unreal operation. Oster’s Asset Setup and Texture Utility series provide related Unreal Python study. Keep the first example bounded rather than constructing a full material system during this lesson.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Qt: small implementation examples
slides.code:
form = QFormLayout()
form.addRow("Source file", source_field)
form.addRow("Destination", target_field)

source_field.textChanged.connect(update_preview)
import_button.clicked.connect(run_import)
bullets: Layouts express relationships
Signals connect actions and feedback
slides.question: Which UX decision does each line support?
slides.notes: These are illustrative fragments requiring surrounding widget setup and callbacks. They are not a complete importer. Qt can illustrate general Python GUI concepts while Editor Utility Widgets provide an Unreal-native comparison. Neither toolkit determines the quality of the workflow on its own.
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Other production references
slides.question: Which workflow problem transfers to your own tool?
slides.notes: Ubisoft’s GDC session describes the Pylon release tool’s UX redesign before Rainbow Six Extraction. Epic’s Fortnite Tools and Ryan’s batch-renaming tutorial provide different editor examples. Compare the user’s task and the evidence each tool exposes. These examples use different technologies and should not be treated as one Python pipeline.
links: Fortnite Tools: inspect and locate overlaps
slides.rationale: Retain the topic and refine its explanation within the assessment, overview and peer-testing sequence.

slides.title: Unreal production architecture
slides.credit: Etienne Palmer-Campbell · NetherRealm · GDC 2025 · PDF p.26
slides.notes: Mission Kontrol separates its Slate interface from network adapters and game automation. This is a production architecture example, not a Python editor recipe. Compare the separation of responsibilities with our smaller UI and operation model.
slides.question: Which boundary makes independent changes easier?
slides.rationale: Offer technical depth without implying runtime Python support.

slides.title: Existing Unreal widgets as references
slides.credit: Etienne Palmer-Campbell · NetherRealm · GDC 2025 · PDF p.34
slides.notes: The Widget Reflector can inspect Unreal’s Slate widget hierarchy and connect a visible widget to implementation information. Use it as an exploration route when you move beyond the Python and Editor Utility examples in this class.
slides.question: Which familiar editor control could guide your design?
slides.rationale: Provide a professional implementation reference for later Slate work.

slides.title: Shareable reproduction steps
slides.credit: Etienne Palmer-Campbell · NetherRealm · GDC 2025 · PDF p.51
slides.notes: Mission Kontrol supports sharing test scripts as JSON. For your tool, consider saving the input and settings needed to repeat a reported problem. A screenshot of the final failure may not include the starting conditions.
slides.question: What would you attach to a useful bug report?
slides.rationale: Connect data-driven tooling with reproducibility.

slides.title: Production feedback is evidence with limits
slides.credit: Jeff Stewart · Vicarious Visions · GDC 2018 · PDF p.13
slides.notes: This published chart reports Vicarious Visions’ internal workflow survey. Treat it as studio-reported feedback. It does not establish that a single feature caused a productivity gain. In your lab, combine ratings with observed task behavior.
slides.question: What would you need before interpreting this as a causal result?
slides.rationale: Include a real chart while teaching careful interpretation.

slides.title: A production prototype evolves

slides.title: Reveal detail where the artist is looking
slides.credit: Guerrilla · GDC 2017 · published world-map clip · 16 seconds

Ask what can remain visible and what can appear only when needed. For a classroom Unreal tool, the comparable decision might be a concise result list with additional information on selection. This clip demonstrates a production interaction; it does not establish that hover-only information is accessible to everyone. Preserve keyboard and persistent-detail alternatives where needed.
